current_answer: Choose cache policy in this order: decide whether the response is private or safely shared; set explicit browser max-age and, separately, shared-cache s-maxage when needed; add ETag or Last-Modified for cheap validation; then test every request input that can change the body. Under HTTP’s minimum model, a candidate is selected by method plus target URI and may be narrowed by Vary, but Cookie is not automatically part of that key. Set-Cookie alone does not stop caching. A shared cache must not reuse a response to a request carrying Authorization unless the response explicitly permits it with public, s-maxage, or must-revalidate—and that permission is not proof that a user-specific representation is safe to share. Use private, no-cache for personalized browser-local retention, no-store when compliant HTTP caches must not intentionally retain a response, and long-lived public caching only for safe or versioned content. For stale validation, If-None-Match wins whenever it is present: a matching ETag can produce 304, while a nonmatching ETag does not fall back to the date. Diagnose old or wrong content by separating browser/history/service-worker behavior from intermediary evidence and by using redacted A/B markers at the intended hop.

catalogue_card.question: How can web developers choose correct HTTP cache headers and diagnose stale content without accidentally caching private responses?
catalogue_card.text: Separate storage audience, freshness, validation, and variant matching. Use the cache-key/privacy worksheet before sharing responses, and treat hits, Age, and Cache-Status as evidence from a named hop—not as proof of safety.

summary: Fresh reuse may make no network request; stale reuse usually leads to validation.
304 keeps the stored representation while 200 replaces it; If-None-Match takes precedence over If-Modified-Since.
The minimum cache-selection model is method plus target URI; query components normally make distinct targets, but extra normalization/keying is deployment-specific.
Vary constrains matching of nominated request fields, including missing versus present values; Vary: * fails ordinary matching without revalidation.
Cookie is not automatically part of the HTTP minimum key, and Set-Cookie alone is not a cache barrier; personalized bodies should start private.
Authorization needs explicit shared-reuse permission (public, s-maxage, or must-revalidate), but permission is not proof that a user-specific body is safe to share.
A redacted A/B marker plus same-hop Cache-Control, Vary, Set-Cookie, Age, Cache-Status, and Via evidence is a practical pre-deploy check.
The new cache-key outcomes come from a clearly labeled local model, not a live browser, origin, CDN, or shared-cache measurement.
uncertainty: The cache-key worksheet and model outcomes are standards-based expectations and synthetic model output; no live curl/socket capture was available for this run.
Standards do not force every cache to store or reuse a response; browser, service-worker, CDN, reverse-proxy, framework, partitioning, and vendor behavior varies.
The minimum key does not prescribe query normalization or other extra key material; Vary cannot cover unlisted application state.
Age and Cache-Status are useful only when exposed by the responding path; their absence is not proof that no cache exists or that an origin was contacted.
Authorization permission, Vary: Cookie, a 200/304, or a model hit is not a confidentiality guarantee and cannot establish absence of leakage.
freshness_note: The dated HTTP caching basics baseline and validator follow-up remain accessible as source material; this 16 Sep 2026 follow-up adds the narrow cache-key/privacy worksheet, Authorization and Cookie distinctions, and a separate local-model limitation without replacing either report.
